title: The Experience Curve
equation: New Cost = Old Cost × Learning Rate ^ (Doublings)
hook: Your first hundred units will always cost more than they should. That's normal.
statement: Every time your total output doubles, your cost per unit drops by a steady percentage.
explainer: Costs fall with reps, not with time. So price for the volume you're heading toward, not the clunky early numbers you're stuck with today.
sop: Find your cost per unit at two points where total output roughly doubled.
Divide the later cost by the earlier one to get your Learning Rate.
Estimate how many more Doublings are realistic.
Project your New Cost and set pricing against it.
equation_example: Old Cost $100, Learning Rate 0.85, 3 more Doublings. $100 × 0.85 × 0.85 × 0.85 = $61.41 per unit. A lower Learning Rate means steeper savings. A rate close to 1 means experience barely helps.
question: Write down what one unit cost you a year ago and what it costs now.
closing_statement: Every doubling of reps makes the expensive stuff cheaper.
caption:
Principle Nº 330: The Experience Curve

Your first hundred units will always cost more than they should. That's normal.

Every time your total output doubles, your cost per unit drops by a steady percentage.
